title: ORMs, migrations and the N+1 problem

videos.script: Ten lessons at a prompt, typing SQL. Almost nobody who builds an application does that. They write in a language, the language has objects, and something in between turns a method call into a statement. That something is the subject of this lesson. {{orm}} It is a good tool. It sends values separately from the statement, so a user cannot type SQL into your query. It keeps the types straight. It writes the boring statements for you. And it carries your schema from one version to the next. {{gifts}} What it does not do is make SQL go away. Every method call is a statement the database runs and charges for, and the statement is not always the one the code looks like. {{emits}} Here is the famous case. Four lines that list fifty customers and their orders. They run fifty-one queries. Nothing in the four lines says so. On the developer's machine it is fine; on production, with five thousand customers, it is five thousand and one, and the page times out. {{nplusone}} So the first half of the lesson is how to see what the mapper sent, and the handful of places where what it sent is not what you would guess. {{see}} The second half is the schema. Migrations: the change written as a file, run once everywhere, never edited afterwards. And the question of who owns the rules — the class that describes the table, or the table itself. {{schema}} The answer is the table. The class is a picture of it. {{table}}
